profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal brainstorming meeting at a London commercial law firm between the Construction team and the Legal Innovation team. Context: several contractor and developer clients have recently asked whether blockchain-based smart contracts could realistically be used in UK construction, and a new paper on stakeholder perceptions has given the firm a timely hook for a client roundtable and follow-up briefing note. Agenda: identify which stakeholder groups the roundtable should speak to, generate a shortlist of plausible early smart-contract use cases in construction, and decide what kind of supporting material the firm should prepare. Expected outcome: a rough concept for a client-facing session, plus 2-3 candidate use cases and a plan for a short discussion note.

members.name: Eleanor Price
members.expertise: UK construction contracts, payment mechanisms, adjudication, JCT and NEC drafting, contentious and non-contentious project advice
members.background: Eleanor has spent 16 years advising developers, main contractors, and consultants on major building and infrastructure projects, with a practice built around payment disputes, contract administration, and risk allocation under standard forms.
members.private_state: She wants the firm's output to feel commercially grounded and immediately credible to conservative construction clients, and she is wary of framing anything as more implementable than it really is under current UK law and market practice.
hidden_assumptions: "Stakeholders" in this context mainly means the project participants with direct contractual exposure, such as employers, main contractors, subcontractors, consultants, and certifiers.
A "viable" smart-contract use case is one that could be deployed in live UK projects under current legal frameworks and familiar JCT/NEC structures without major bespoke redesign.
When the team says they should "map the payment workflow," the exercise is primarily a legal one about notices, certification steps, withholding positions, and adjudication triggers.
"Supply-type contracts" refers to relatively clean supply-only or off-site goods packages with objective delivery and payment milestones, not mixed service arrangements.

members.name: Ravi Shah
members.expertise: Smart contracts, blockchain implementation, legal operations design, fintech product structuring, emerging technology governance
members.background: Ravi trained in commercial technology law, spent several years advising fintech clients on blockchain products, and now works inside the firm's innovation group helping practice teams design client-facing offerings around automation and digital contracting.
members.private_state: He wants to turn the discussion into a visible cross-practice initiative and is looking for a pilot-friendly angle that shows the firm is forward-looking, even if it starts in a controlled or bespoke environment rather than mainstream deployment.
hidden_assumptions: "Stakeholders" naturally includes implementation actors beyond the immediate contracting chain, such as software vendors, insurers, lenders, platform providers, and independent certifiers.
A "viable" use case can be one that is suitable for a limited pilot or sandbox with bespoke clauses and governance, even if it is not yet ready for standard-form market adoption.
When the team says they should "map the payment workflow," the work mainly involves identifying operational data inputs, system triggers, oracle logic, and release conditions for automated execution.
"Supply-type contracts" can include standardized ancillary arrangements such as plant hire, logistics, and planned maintenance packages, provided the inputs are structured enough to automate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss "stakeholders" and "who the roundtable is for" as though they mean the same audience.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the core construction participants with direct project contracts or direct administration roles: clients, main contractors, subcontractors, consultants, and contract administrators/certifiers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the wider adoption ecosystem as well, including insurers, funders, software vendors, platform providers, and others who shape whether smart contracts can be implemented.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal and industry discussions, "stakeholders" is routinely used as an umbrella term, so both speakers can keep building on the conversation without noticing that one has a narrow legal-privity frame and the other a broader implementation frame.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes a use case viable
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should identify a "viable first use case" or "low-friction option."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a use case that clients could realistically deploy soon on live projects under current UK construction law and recognizable standard-form documentation, with limited drafting novelty.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a use case that is realistic enough for a controlled pilot or proof-of-concept, even if it requires bespoke terms, a closed user group, or non-standard governance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Brainstorming language like "first use case" and "low-friction" sounds aligned because both are trying to avoid overly ambitious automation, but their thresholds for real-world readiness differ in a way that does not need to be stated for the conversation to feel smooth.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to map the payment workflow
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they should "map the payment workflow" before developing materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a legal process map showing payment notices, certification, due dates, pay less notices, and dispute escalation points under UK construction payment rules.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an operational systems map showing what data source triggers payment, how completion or delivery is verified, what oracle or platform records the event, and how an automated release occurs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Process mapping is such an ordinary preliminary step that neither expects ambiguity; each assumes the other is simply endorsing the obvious groundwork, even though they are imagining different artifacts.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to smart contracts being most plausible for "simple supply-type contracts."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes straightforward supply-only arrangements, especially goods or off-site manufactured components with clear delivery and acceptance events.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes broader standardized packages around projects, such as plant hire, logistics, consumables replenishment, and planned maintenance where event data can be structured.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The paper itself frames supply-type contracts as the obvious early category, so both can use the phrase approvingly while silently drawing different boundaries around which arrangements belong inside it.

turns.inner_thought: This is a useful opening if we keep it disciplined. Clients are asking whether smart contracts are real in UK construction, but I do not want us promising some futuristic rollout that ignores the Housing Grants regime, notice mechanics, certification, or how JCT and NEC projects are actually administered. If we pitch this roundtable around a viable first use case, it needs to mean something clients could actually recognise and deploy soon, not an innovation lab exercise dressed up as market-ready.
turns.utterance: I think we have a good opening for a client roundtable here. There is definitely curiosity in the market, but if we do it, it needs to stay practical and tied to current UK construction concerns. I'd be keen that we frame it around what a viable first use case might actually look like, rather than starting with the most ambitious version of the idea.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she wants practical framing, and I can work with that. The paper gives us more than a legal hook: it lets us talk about why adoption stalls, who needs to trust the process, and what conditions make automation acceptable. When I say stakeholders, I want the room to include the wider implementation ecosystem too, because without platform providers, insurers, funders and the rest, the conversation risks becoming doctrinal and static.
turns.utterance: Yes, and what I liked about the paper is that it gives us a neat way into the human side of it. It is not just about black-letter analysis; it shows how different stakeholders respond to automation, where the hesitation sits, and what would need to be in place before people are comfortable moving beyond theory.

turns.inner_thought: We should keep the audience anchored in the participants my construction clients immediately recognise. If the roundtable becomes too diffuse, it will lose relevance. For me the key stakeholders are the parties actually administering and bearing payment risk on projects: employers, main contractors, subcontractors, consultants, and the people issuing or relying on certificates.
turns.utterance: I agree. For the session itself, though, I think we should centre the discussion on the stakeholders our construction clients will immediately recognise. If the examples speak clearly to employers, main contractors, consultants and subcontractors, the conversation will feel grounded from the outset.

turns.inner_thought: That works as a core audience, but I do not want us to miss the actors who make implementation possible or impossible. In any pilot or controlled deployment, the practical blockers often sit with insurers, software vendors, platform operators, lenders and independent verification roles. I can add that without sounding like I am changing the frame entirely.
turns.utterance: Absolutely, and I think that same stakeholder lens can still be a bit wider when we shape the agenda. It would be helpful to bring in the parties who affect whether the model is workable in practice as well, so we are not looking at it only through the immediate project documents.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, as long as the discussion does not drift too far from live construction contracting. We should keep everyone focused on one or two viable first use cases, and simple supply-type contracts are the obvious starting point because they are cleaner, more objective, and less entangled with valuation and service performance. I am thinking straightforward goods or off-site manufacture, not messy hybrid arrangements.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. To keep it manageable, I think the roundtable should work toward one or two viable first use cases. My instinct is that simple supply-type contracts are probably the cleanest place to start, because they let us test the idea in a relatively contained setting.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that gives me space to steer toward candidates that are structured enough for a pilot. In my mind, supply-type contracts comfortably covers plant hire, logistics flows, consumables and repeat maintenance packages, because those have routine events and cleaner data. If we can land on one of those, we could turn this into a visible cross-practice pilot conversation quite quickly.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that is the right category. Within simple supply-type contracts, there are a few examples that feel like viable early candidates because the process is relatively repeatable and the commercial events are easier to organise. That gives us something concrete to put in front of clients without overreaching.

turns.inner_thought: Before we start naming examples too confidently, I want the legal architecture set out properly. We need a payment process map showing due dates, notices, certification points, withholding positions and where disputes bite, otherwise the whole thing risks sounding detached from the statutory and contractual payment machinery construction clients actually deal with.
turns.utterance: Before we get too specific on examples, I do think we should map the payment workflow first. That will help us show where the key steps sit, where pressure points might arise, and how any proposed use case would fit into a recognisable process.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. For me that mapping exercise is where the offering becomes real: identify the event inputs, handoffs, verification points, and release conditions so we can show what would actually happen operationally when payment moves. If we can produce a clear workflow diagram, it will support both the roundtable and a later pilot conversation.
turns.utterance: I completely agree. If we map the payment workflow properly, we can show not just the process on paper but also what would need to happen at each stage for the mechanism to work cleanly. That should make the discussion much more tangible for the room.

turns.inner_thought: The client-facing message has to be conservative and credible. I want them leaving with a low-friction option that feels achievable within existing contracting habits, not with the sense that they need to redesign their procurement model or take untested legal risk. If we strike that tone, the construction team can stand behind it.
turns.utterance: And I think the eventual takeaway needs to be a low-friction option. Clients should come away feeling that there is an achievable route in, rather than that they would need to rewrite their contracting habits overnight to get any value from this.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I can package this as a short note that ties the stakeholder picture to a pilot-style workflow and tees up the roundtable. If we anchor it around a simple supply package, we can keep it concrete while still opening the door to a broader innovation initiative later. She will read 'pilot-style' as illustrative; I mean something we could actually test in a controlled environment.
turns.utterance: In that case, perhaps the next step is a short discussion note ahead of the session. We could link the stakeholder picture to a workflow diagram for a simple supply-type contract, set out the main questions for discussion, and use that as the basis for the roundtable conversation.
